title: From Hot Pink to Green: Katydid's Color Shift Baffles Scientists
summary: In the dense rainforests of Panama, a surprising discovery is rewriting what we know about insect camouflage. Researchers have documented a katydid — a leaf-mimicking insect also called a bush cricket — that changed its entire body color from bright hot pink to green in just eleven days. The finding, published in the journal Ecology, suggests this rapid transformation is not a genetic fluke but a sophisticated survival strategy. The katydid, identified as Arota festae, was found on Barro Colorado Island by scientists from the University of St Andrews, University of Reading, and other institutions. When first spotted under a light, the adult female was a striking hot pink. But within four days, the color began to fade to a pastel shade, and by day eleven, she was indistinguishable from the typical green form. "Rather than a bizarre genetic quirk, this may actually be a finely tuned survival strategy that tracks the life cycle of the rainforest leaves this insect is trying to resemble," said lead author Dr. Benito Wainwright. The key lies in a phenomenon called "delayed greening," where new tropical leaves emerge in pink or red hues before turning green. On Barro Colorado Island, about one-third of plant species exhibit this pattern, providing a consistent backdrop of pink foliage. A katydid that can shift from pink to green could seamlessly blend in with both young and mature leaves, avoiding predators like birds and lizards. Previously, pink katydids were considered rare, disadvantageous mutations. This is the first recorded instance of a katydid completing a full color transition within a single life stage. Co-author Dr. Matt Greenwell noted, "You would think that a bright pink insect in a mostly green forest would stand out to predators like a worker in a high-vis jacket. But this is a remarkable example of camouflage in action." The insect lived long enough to mate and died naturally a month later. The discovery hints at the extraordinary, still-hidden adaptations in tropical ecosystems, where even the colors of leaves can shape the evolution of the creatures that hide among them.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that even in a well-studied rainforest, nature still holds remarkable tricks — a reminder that camouflage is an active, shapeshifting arms race, and that losing even one species could mean losing unique survival strategies we haven’t yet understood or learned from.

background_read: Barro Colorado Island, created by the damming of the Panama Canal in 1914, has become one of the most intensively studied tropical ecosystems on Earth, run by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute.

Katydids, including the species Arota festae, belong to a group of insects famous for their leaf-like wings and body patterns — an extreme form of plant-mimicking camouflage that fools birds and lizards.

The phenomenon of delayed greening, where young tropical leaves flush pink or red before turning green, is thought to protect against herbivores or intense sunlight; on Barro Colorado Island about one-third of plant species show this pattern.

Historically, pink katydids were dismissed as rare, disadvantageous mutations doomed to be eaten; this study, published in the journal Ecology, is the first to record a full color switch within a single adult’s lifetime.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — A breakthrough in understanding rapid adaptation
perspectives.description: The finding reveals that a single insect can flexibly match its environment within its lifetime, overturning the idea that pink katydids are helpless mutants; this could inspire new materials that change color on demand.
Such finely tuned camouflage depends on a specific mix of leaf colors; deforestation or climate shifts that alter the timing of leaf flush could break this survival strategy, endangering the species.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — A case of phenotypic plasticity
perspectives.description: From an analytical viewpoint, this is an example of phenotypic plasticity — an organism’s ability to change its physical traits in response to environmental cues. It adds to a growing database of how animals use flexible disguise rather than fixed coloring.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — A call for deeper field study
perspectives.description: Scientists argue that many more such rapid changes likely go unnoticed in tropical forests; future research using high-frequency monitoring could uncover a hidden layer of dynamic camouflage and inform conservation priorities.
